Apple has long made privacy a selling point for its hardware and services, but I sometimes wonder if it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

A measure that looks limited in scope has been challenged every few months by a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator. The UK has now seen a third lawsuit involving ATT—and this one has something a little different about it.

Apple's response was added at the end of the article...

The personalised advertising debate

Personalised advertising has been a hot topic in tech for years. Rather than showing us random ads we may have zero interest in, why not show us ads based on our interests—gleaned from the apps we use and the sites we visit?

In theory, this is good for everyone. Consumers see ads they may actually be interested in; advertisers get a better return on their spend because they can target more precisely; and the free apps and websites that rely on ad revenue also get more money for the same reason.

Even though the data used to deliver personalised ads is collected anonymously, the practice is widely seen by the public as an invasion of privacy. Even though Apple specifically developed a technology to make sure that data is anonymous, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency was intended to solve this problem by giving consumers a choice. Developers who want to collect such data must first get the consumer's consent.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, the measure has attracted a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, largely because Apple's own apps don't have to ask for that same consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules are consistent: its own apps don't show the ATT prompt because they don't collect such data in the first place. Third-party apps that don't collect such data are also exempt and don't show the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints filed with the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal, the relevant antitrust regulator. It lost the first case and is currently appealing; the second is ongoing.

The third lawsuit was reported by Reuters and was officially filed today.

What's new

The latest lawsuit has an interesting twist: the claimant is Ann Pope, a former senior official at the regulator behind this very case.

Ann Pope, who is leading the lawsuit, was previously a senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority. She says Apple's policies "have caused very significant harm to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." In a statement, Pope said: "This action is important to safeguard the rights of UK businesses that rely on Apple, to ensure the rules Apple applies are fair and to compensate UK companies for the losses they have suffered."
